You learn the casual style (ふつうけい), the way Japanese people speak with family, friends and children: だ instead of です, the dictionary form instead of ～ます, questions without か.
right? / you know (very common in casual speech)
To understand the difference between the polite style (です / ます) and the casual style (だ / the dictionary form).
To change verbs: いきます → いく, いきません → いかない, いきました → いった, いきませんでした → いかなかった.
To change adjectives and nouns: たかい です → たかい, げんき です → げんき だ.
To ask casual questions, without か, just with intonation.
To know WHO you can speak casually with and who you can’t.
Mihai and Ana have arrived in Hiroshima, at Kenji’s house. Haruka welcomes them, and her daughter, Sakura (8), talks to them casually, the way children do.
Thank you for having us. These are souvenirs from Spain.
Hey, hey! Did you come from Spain?
Yes, that’s right. I live in Madrid.
Cool! It’s the same city as Daddy! And you?
I’m Romanian. But I live in Madrid now.
Romania? Where’s that? Is it far?
Yes, very far. About fifteen hours by plane, I think.
Sakura, speak politely to our guests.
No, it’s fine. Sakura’s Japanese is teaching us a lot.
Hey, are you hungry? Mummy’s okonomiyaki is super yummy!
Really? I want to eat it! Is it better than Kenji’s ramen?
Yeah! I like Daddy’s ramen too, but Mummy’s is better. It’s a secret!
Hee-hee. Then I’ll make it right away. Please wait a moment.
While we’re waiting, let’s play! We have three dogs. They’re not dangerous.
Yes, let’s play! What are the dogs called?
“ojama shimasu” = excuse me for intruding (when entering someone’s home)
“benkyō ni narimasu” = it teaches us a lot
we wait (casual for まって いる)
let’s play (casual for あそびましょう)
Without か, a question is made just with your voice rising at the end: いく?↗ (are you going?) versus いく。↘ (I’m going).
うん (yeah) is short, with a falling voice. ううん (no) has two syllables, with the voice high-low: u-UN. Careful, they’re easy to confuse!
In casual speech, ～て いる becomes ～てる: まって いる → まってる, たべて いる → たべてる.

Until now you’ve only spoken politely (です / ます). That’s the right style with strangers, colleagues, bosses and shop assistants. But with family, close friends and children, Japanese people speak CASUALLY (ふつうけい, the plain form).
The good news: you already know them all! The dictionary form (chapter 14), the ～ない form (15) and the ～た form (16) ARE the casual forms. Only “didn’t do” is new: ～なかった.
2. Adjectives and nouns in casual speech
げんき だ (or just げんき)
With -い adjectives you DON’T add だ: “たかい だ” is wrong! Just say たかい.
Girls and women often leave out だ: げんき よ, そう よ. Boys often keep だ: げんき だよ, そう だ.
In the casual style, か is almost always dropped. A question is made with intonation alone (your voice rises):
How are you? / Are you OK?
Where are you going? (even the particle へ can drop)
For “let’s…!” the casual form is ～おう / ～よう: いきましょう → いこう, たべましょう → たべよう, あそびましょう → あそぼう.
For “yes / no”: うん / ううん (instead of はい / いいえ).
4. Who do you speak casually with?
people you’re meeting for the first time
children (and children speak casually to everyone)
colleagues your own age, once you’ve become friends
The golden rule for foreigners: when in doubt, speak POLITELY. Casual speech with a stranger sounds rude. Polite speech with a friend just sounds a little cold, which is a much smaller mistake.
In the dialogue: Haruka (the host) speaks politely to the guests. Sakura (a child) speaks casually. Ana and Mihai speak casually WITH SAKURA (she’s a child), but politely with Haruka.
5. Sentence-final particles: よ, ね, かな
In casual speech, the particles at the end of the sentence add emotional “colour”:
I’m giving you new information (“you know”)
おいしい よ! (It’s tasty, you know!)
さむい ね。(It’s cold, isn’t it?)
I’m confirming something we both know
あした だ よね? (It’s tomorrow, right?)
あめ かな。(I wonder if it’ll rain.)
Without よ and ね, casual Japanese sounds cold and robotic. Listen to how Sakura uses them in the dialogue: in almost every sentence!

さくら の にっき — Sakura’s diary
In the evening, Sakura writes her diary. Japanese children write their diaries in the casual style.
Today Daddy’s friends came from Spain.
Ana is Spanish and she’s really kind. She had long, beautiful hair.
Mihai is Romanian. Romania is really far away. I didn’t know.
They both spoke Japanese well. But sometimes they used funny Japanese. It was fun.
Mihai ate three of Mummy’s okonomiyaki! I was surprised.
And the dogs really loved them both. Madrid slept on Ana’s lap.
Tomorrow we’re going to Miyajima together. They say there are lots of deer. I can’t wait!
I want to see Daddy soon.
loved (“daisuki ni natta” = came to love)
Where did Madrid the dog sleep?
みやじま の しか — The deer of Miyajima
The next day they all went to Miyajima. Ten minutes by boat.
From the boat you could see a huge red torii gate standing in the sea.
“Wow! It’s a gate in the middle of the sea!” said Ana.
“See? It’s one of the most beautiful views in Japan!” said Sakura.
When they arrived on the island, the deer came straight away. One, two, three…
The deer aren’t scared at all. They come right up to people.
“How cute!” Ana stroked a deer on the head.
“Watch out! The deer eat maps too!” Sakura shouted.
Too late. Mihai’s map was already in a deer’s mouth.
Mihai ran after the deer. The deer ran off as fast as its legs could carry it.
Sakura was in fits of laughter. “You’re so funny!”
Haruka said, laughing too: “Never mind. I know the island well.”
At lunchtime they all ate anago-meshi, a famous Miyajima dish.
“Yeah, anago. It’s a fish like an eel. Is it good?”
Without realising it, Mihai was already speaking casually with Sakura.
In the afternoon, Sakura took Ana by the hand and led her to a small shop.
“Let’s buy momiji-manjū here! Because Daddy likes them.”
Sakura went quiet for a moment.
“Yeah, lots. But he’s always far away. Spain is too far.”
Ana crouched down and looked Sakura in the eyes.
“In Madrid, your daddy is always talking about you.”
“Really. He has one of your drawings stuck on the wall of the restaurant.”
Just then Mihai came back. He was holding the wet map.
“I got it back! Only half of it, mind you…”
Half the map was missing. The deer had eaten it.
On the boat back, Sakura fell asleep.
She was holding the box of momiji-manjū tightly in her hands.
“Thank you. Sakura hasn’t laughed like that in a long time.”
The sunset coloured the sea red. The torii gate stood quietly in the middle of the sea.
Mihai put the half map in his pocket. It had become a lovely memory.
That evening, Sakura wrote in her diary: “Today was the best day. The deer was naughty, but it was fun.”
“Daddy, come home soon. Because I want to hear more about Madrid.”
With her little fingers, Sakura also drew a cat. It looked just like Tama.
“onaka o kakaete warau” = to be in fits of laughter
talk (“no hanashi o suru” = to talk about)
What is special about the torii gate at Miyajima?
Her father is always far away
What did Ana tell Sakura to cheer her up?
Her father has one of her drawings on the restaurant wall
